module_title: Recent Heavyweights: Electoral Bonds, Immunity & Sub-classification (2023-2026)
introduction: Tailored for current affairs, UPSC Mains, and advanced legal exams, this level dissects the most explosive and heavily tested Supreme Court Constitutional Bench rulings from the past 24-36 months. These cases have redefined electoral transparency, parliamentary privileges, and reservation policies.

core_concepts.title: Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) v. Union of India (Feb 2024)
core_concepts.description:
The Electoral Bonds Judgment.
- The Issue: The constitutional validity of the anonymous Electoral Bonds scheme, which allowed limitless corporate funding to political parties.
- The Judgment: A 5-judge bench unanimously **struck down the Electoral Bonds Scheme** as unconstitutional. The Court ruled that anonymous political funding violates the voter's Fundamental Right to Information under Article 19(1)(a). The Court held that the scheme failed the proportionality test and disproportionately favored the ruling party, ordering the SBI to publish all donor details.

core_concepts.title: Sita Soren v. Union of India (March 2024)
core_concepts.description:
Overruling the PV Narasimha Rao (1998) Judgment on Parliamentary Immunity.
- The Issue: Can MPs and MLAs claim immunity under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) from criminal prosecution if they take a bribe to cast a vote or make a speech in the House?
- The Judgment: A 7-judge bench unanimously ruled **NO**. Overruling its 1998 precedent, the Court held that bribery is not protected by parliamentary privilege. The act of taking a bribe is complete the moment the money is accepted, independent of how the vote is actually cast. Privilege only protects legitimate legislative functions, not corruption.

core_concepts.title: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (August 2024)
core_concepts.description:
The Sub-classification of SCs/STs.
- The Issue: Can state governments sub-classify Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) to grant separate quotas for the most backward among them? Does it violate the E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) ruling?
- The Judgment: A 7-judge bench (6:1) overruled the 2004 judgment, holding that State governments **CAN sub-classify SCs and STs** to ensure that reservations reach the most marginalized groups within these categories. The Court noted that SCs/STs are not a homogeneous class, and substantive equality demands targeting the weakest.

core_concepts.title: Supriyo v. Union of India (Oct 2023)
core_concepts.description:
The Same-Sex Marriage Judgment.
- The Issue: Petitions seeking legal recognition for same-sex marriages under the Special Marriage Act (SMA).
- The Judgment: A 5-judge bench (3:2 on some issues, unanimous on others) refused to strike down or read words into the SMA to include same-sex marriage, ruling that creating the institution of marriage is strictly a matter for the **Legislature (Parliament)**, not the Judiciary. However, the Court unanimously recognized the right of queer couples to cohabit free from discrimination.

important_entities.name: Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL (July 2024)
important_entities.key_fact: A massive victory for Fiscal Federalism.
important_entities.significance: A 9-judge bench ruled (8:1) that State governments have the absolute constitutional power to tax mineral rights. The Court held that 'royalty' is not a tax, and the Central law (MMDR Act) does not strip states of their fiscal powers under Entry 50 of List II. This resulted in thousands of crores in back-taxes being owed to mineral-rich states.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Did the Supreme Court merely ban the future sale of Electoral Bonds? **NO**. The Court ordered the complete unmasking of the scheme, requiring the State Bank of India (SBI) and the Election Commission of India (ECI) to retrospectively publish the alpha-numeric codes matching every corporate donor to the exact political party that encashed the bond since 2019.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: ADR = Transparency; Sita Soren = Accountability; Davinder = Equality; MADA = Federalism
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Link the 2024 case name to the core constitutional principle it strengthened.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains GS-2, when discussing the intersection of corruption and parliamentary privileges, you must center your answer on the **Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)** judgment and how it rectifies the historical error of the 1998 PV Narasimha Rao case.
